content: Hyperpyrexia is defined as an abnormally high elevation of the body’s core temperature, reaching or exceeding 41.1°C (106°F). This condition represents an extreme form of fever and is distinct from hyperthermia. In hyperpyrexia, the body’s thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus actively sets the temperature to an abnormally high level, whereas in hyperthermia, the body’s temperature exceeds the set point due to external or environmental factors. Several conditions and factors can lead to hyperpyrexia, including: Stimulant abuse: The use of amphetamines or other stimulants can exacerbate the effects of heat hyperpyrexia by increasing metabolic activity and impairing thermoregulation. Substance withdrawal: Withdrawal from substances such as barbiturates, alcohol, or other anxiolytics can occasionally result in hyperpyrexia. However, this is less commonly observed with benzodiazepine withdrawal. Septicemia: A systemic bacterial infection of the bloodstream can provoke hyperpyrexia as part of the body’s inflammatory response to severe infection. Certain viral infections: Viral illnesses, such as infectious mononucleosis, can also lead to hyperpyrexia in some cases. Thyrotoxic crisis: In individuals with hyperthyroidism, a thyrotoxic crisis can result in hyperpyrexia due to excessive thyroid hormone activity, which increases metabolic heat production. Malignant hyperpyrexia: This is a specific condition characterized by muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) following extreme muscle excitation. It can be triggered by factors such as intense physical exertion in high ambient temperatures, prolonged seizures, certain anesthetic agents, or the use of drugs like cocaine, alcohol, or aspirin. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): This life-threatening condition can occur after the administration of antipsychotic medications. It is associated with hyperpyrexia, muscle rigidity, autonomic dysregulation, and altered mental status. Each of these causes requires careful clinical evaluation and management to address the underlying condition and mitigate the risks associated with extreme elevations in body temperature.
